The 2030 set is the 2026 set: the four-year terms elected in 2026 end in January 2031 (December 2030 in Alaska and Hawaii), and New Hampshire and Vermont elect every two years. Neither state's 2026 ballot carried a four-year-term amendment.

senate: Class 3 (34 seats) is up in 2028 and again in 2034, Class 1 (33) in 2030 and again in 2036, Class 2 (33) in 2032. The counts match the task brief.

2034 (added 2026-11-05) reuses the Class 3 seats listed for 2028. The incumbents are informational only (the generic markets name nobody); a special election or vacancy before 2034 does not change which seats are up.

Class 1 for 2030 was re-verified on 2026-11-05: senate.gov's class pages answer automated requests with HTTP 403 that day, so the 33 states were checked against the congress-legislators file and Wikipedia's 2030 page instead. Same 33 states as on 2026-10-06.

No special Senate election is scheduled for 2030 as of 2026-11-05. Two Class 1 senators were their party's nominees for governor on 2026-11-03 (Minnesota, Tennessee): a senator who becomes governor leaves the seat to an appointee and a special election for the rest of the term ending January 3, 2031, which is a different term from the 2030 regular election and is not in this inventory. Add a 2030 special when one is called.

The Florida and Ohio Class 3 seats are filled by appointees (Moody, Husted) until the November 3, 2026 special elections; those specials cover the unexpired terms ending January 3, 2029, so both seats have their regular full-term election in 2028 as part of Class 3. They are not extra 2028 seats.
Special elections for seats vacated after this inventory was written are out of scope; add them when they are called, as the brief says.

Vermont has no Class 2 seat and Nebraska/Alaska have no Class 3 / Class 1 seat respectively, so the 'Another party or independent' exceptions in SEEDS.md apply only to the cycles in which those states actually vote.
governors: The brief expected the 36 states of the 2026 cycle; confirmed: AK, AL, AR, AZ, CA, CO, CT, FL, GA, HI, IA, ID, IL, KS, MA, MD, ME, MI, MN, NE, NH, NM, NV, NY, OH, OK, OR, PA, RI, SC, SD, TN, TX, VT, WI, WY.
Kentucky, Louisiana and Mississippi (2027) and New Jersey and Virginia (2029) elect governors in odd years; territories are out of scope.

Incumbents are as of October 2026 (before the 2026-11-03 elections) and informational only, cross-checked against the 2026 launch audit (backend/scripts/elections-2026/audit/race-inventory.json, 2026-10-03). Every one of these seats was on the 2026 ballot, so the 2030 incumbents are the 2026 winners (New Hampshire's and Vermont's, the 2028 winners); 2026 results are not recorded here.

Alaska and Hawaii governors take office on the first Monday in December after the election (Alaska Const. art. III, § 4; Hawaii Const. art. V, § 1): December 2, 2030. Every other state's term begins in January 2031.
Georgia: a majority is required; otherwise a runoff between the top two on the 28th day after the general (O.C.G.A. § 21-2-501): December 3, 2030.
Alaska: top-four primary and ranked-choice general (2020 Ballot Measure 2); a repeal initiative was on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
California: top-two primary; the general is between the two candidates who advance (plurality of the two).
Maine: the general election for governor is decided by plurality; Maine's ranked-choice voting covers primaries and federal general elections only (the 2026 launch audit applied the same rule).
Vermont: Vt. Const. ch. II, § 47 — if no candidate has a majority, the General Assembly elects the governor from the top three by joint ballot in January.
Minnesota's Democratic Party is the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL); recorded as D below.
